knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x-{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln(4),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2-3{x}^{2}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={4}^{u}\ln(4)\cdot (2-3{x}^{2}) \\ & =(2-3{x}^{2})\cdot {4}^{u}\ln(4) \\ & =(2-3{x}^{2})\cdot {4}^{2x-{x}^{3}}\ln(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=1} & =(2-3(1)^{2})\cdot {4}^{2(1)-(1)^{3}}\ln(4) \\ & =-1\cdot {4}^{1}\ln(4) \\ & =- 4 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is $- 4 \ln{\left(4 \right)}.$
